title: Without the crowd
hookLine: the singer is only anxious when he wants the crowd's applause (Discourses 2.13)

lines: IN THE SHOWER, YOU CAN SING.
cards: In the shower, a person can sing. Really sing. Full voice, the high note, the whole song.
Then someone hands that same person a microphone at a wedding, and the throat closes up. The voice didn't change between the bathroom and the reception hall. Neither did the skill.
Something else walked into the room. Epictetus describes this exact moment, with a singer in a theater, and he names what walked in.

teach.h: WHAT DOES THE ANXIOUS ONE WANT?
teach.b: This is Discourses book two, chapter thirteen, on anxiety. Epictetus starts like a doctor making a diagnosis. When I see someone anxious, he says, I ask: what does this person want?
If they didn't want something outside their control, why would they be anxious? Then the musician. A lyre player singing by himself isn't anxious at all.

teach.h: ALONE: NO ANXIETY. THE THEATER: ANXIETY.
teach.b: But when he walks into the theater, even with a fine voice and beautiful playing, he is. Why? Because he doesn't only want to sing well.
He wants to be applauded, and that isn't up to him. Where his skill is, there's confidence. Bring in a crowd he wants something from, and the anxiety arrives.
Then a pair of real people.
When Zeno, the founder of the Stoic school, went to see King Antigonus, Zeno wasn't anxious. Antigonus was. The king wanted to impress the philosopher; the philosopher wanted nothing from the king.
The one with the power was the one sweating. The fix isn't to stop caring about doing well. Practice your craft, Epictetus says; get good.
The fix is to notice when part of you is singing for the applause, and bring your attention back to the singing.
You can stand in a full room and still, inside, be singing without the crowd.

how: Stoic practitioners often meet nerves by asking what they want that isn't in their control, usually approval, and turning their attention back to doing the task well.

o: the pain of a wound that just won't heal
deep grief at losing someone you love dearly
anxiety: the strain of wanting what isn't up to you

games.q: without the crowd: tap the pairs.
p: the lyre player in the theater

s: Epictetus says anxiety comes from a bad voice or poor skill
the singer has a fine voice; the anxiety comes from wanting applause.
when Zeno met King Antigonus, the king was the anxious one
the king wanted to impress the philosopher, who wanted nothing from him.
Epictetus tells his students to stop caring about doing well
he says practice your craft; just stop singing for the applause.

games.q: you're Zeno, founder of the Stoic school, about to meet King Antigonus. who's anxious?
o: the king, because he wants to impress you.
games.why: Epictetus says Zeno wasn't anxious, Antigonus was: the one who wanted something from the other felt the strain.

practice: Think of something coming up that makes you nervous, a presentation, a meeting, a post, and ask Epictetus' question: what do I want here that isn't up to me? Name it: their approval, their applause.
Then picture doing the thing the way you sing in the shower, and notice any difference in your chest.

wordCard.voice: Agōnia. Greek for the strain of a contest, anxiety: Epictetus' diagnosis of nerves, the singer alone is calm, and the anxiety comes with wanting applause.

orig.note: Greek agōnia: the strain of a contest, anxiety (our word agony); 2.13 is on being anxious.

carryVoice: Your line: singing for the applause. The song was always the point. Day four hundred eleven, done.
